rationale: A wins because it turns the same thin product launch into three clean stories with real editorial tension: "Linear Is Expanding to Product Teams. It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" is a business-model angle, not launch confetti. B is competent, but it pads into softer category mush like "Another roadmapping tool arrives for product teams already drowning in software" and lets "pricing still unset" carry more weight than it has. A also does the grown-up thing: it names proof gaps without pretending the update gave it customer evidence it did not have.
gaps_in_A: "Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows" are plausible competitors, but the update names none; A should mark that as an inference, not state it as if supplied.
"Product managers and designers as a group often want different affordances" is journalistically useful, but still a generalized claim that needs outside proof or softer phrasing.
"The product launch is live as of today" overstates the timing slightly; the update says Linear is launching and gives current time, but not the exact public launch status.
gaps_in_B: "category-creation" is the wrong story type for "Linear bets its engineering-only interface can win over product managers too"; this is product-fit/design-philosophy, not category creation.

"new buyer segment" and "historically sold top-down to VPs" smuggle in assumptions not present in the update. The facts say PMs and designers are the audience; they do not establish the buyer or sales history.
"pricing being unannounced is itself a live, checkable fact" is thin gruel. It is a useful question, not enough to anchor a competitive angle.
"Another roadmapping tool arrives for product teams already drowning in software" relies on tooling-fatigue framing the update does not prove, and it overlaps with the first interface/adoption angle.
